observation: Inference providers must keep many LLMs available, including low-volume but essential models, while token prices fall, making resource efficiency increasingly important. To meet strict SLOs they dedicate GPU groups per model, yet production GPU duty cycles commonly fall below 30%. Analyses of production traces from major inference providers (Hyperbolic, Novita AI) and Chatbot Arena reveal a dynamic, rapidly shifting bursty-group pattern: requests concentrate on a small subset of concurrently active models and that subset changes frequently (23%–50% of models active on average; active set changes 54–766 times per hour), and per-model request streams are extremely volatile with abrupt pattern shifts and many idle intervals. In such conditions pure time sharing causes repeated model swapping, thrashing, and SLO-violating queuing spikes, while pure space sharing leaves memory locked to idle models (in the Novita AI trace models are idle over 70% of the time and roughly 50% of GPU memory is occupied but unused), starving active models during bursts. Thus neither sharing strategy alone can satisfy SLOs and efficiency under realistic multi-LLM workloads; what is needed is a fluid combination of both.

solution.idea:
The central issue is that previous designs reduce multi-LLM serving to an all-or-nothing resource decision at a single time scale. QLM-style time sharing swaps entire model states at the granularity of request groups, so a rapidly changing active set causes repeated, non-amortized weight movement and preemption. MuxServe-style space sharing pins models to GPUs and never reclaims the memory of idle models, so the very memory that could help an active burst is unavailable. ServerlessLLM treats model activation as a cold-start event that happens after a request has already arrived, making latency depend on an expensive load. None of these approaches recognizes that GPU memory and GPU compute are two different resources that can be managed at two different time scales: memory can keep many models resident while compute is dynamically assigned to whichever resident model has urgent work; and idle models can give up memory without requiring the GPU to stop running active models.

We therefore design a fluid, memory-centric scheduler built on a virtualized model-footprint abstraction. A model is no longer an atomic unit that is either present or absent. Its GPU footprint consists of weight pages and KV-cache pages, each independently mappable to physical HBM. Space sharing then means that the weight pages of multiple models are simultaneously resident in the same GPU. Time sharing means that the compute engine switches execution among resident models at batch boundaries, with no weight movement. Eviction and prefetching are driven by a burstiness-aware, two-threshold residency policy rather than by the arrival of the next request group. When the active-set composition shifts, the scheduler changes the compute runnable set immediately and changes the memory-resident set only after a debounce interval, which prevents the thrashing observed in QLM. When a model becomes idle, its pages are retained for a grace period; only if the planner predicts low future demand and another model needs memory are pages reclaimed. Thus pure spatial sharing becomes the extreme where every predicted model is kept resident, pure temporal sharing becomes the extreme where only one model's pages fit and others must be loaded, and ordinary operation is a middle regime where co-resident models share HBM while a request-level scheduler allocates GPU cycles to active queues.

The trade-off is between memory footprint and cold-start risk: keeping more pages resident consumes memory that could otherwise be used for KV cache or additional replicas, while evicting too eagerly reintroduces cold-start latency. We resolve this with hysteresis plus an explicit utility score that weighs current queue pressure, predicted near-future demand, checkpoint locality, and the cost of loading. We also avoid two common alternatives we considered and rejected: prefill-decode disaggregation such as Aegaeon, because it duplicates weights and needs a stable active-mode structure that the observed dynamic group pattern does not have, and monolithic virtual-memory reimplementation such as vAttention/vTensor as an end in itself, because the key problem is not virtual memory but a scheduler that exploits virtual mappings to fluidly combine memory and compute sharing. We instead use virtual mapping as a mechanism underneath a model-level resident/runnable state machine.
solution.implementation:
The system has five cooperating components: a workload monitor, a two-tier resource view, a residency planner, an eviction/prefetch engine, and a request-level GPU scheduler.

1. Resource abstraction and model footprints. Each model m has a logical address space of weight pages and KV pages. Weight pages are read-only and have a permanent clean copy in a local checkpoint, laid out with the checkpoint locality used by ServerlessLLM. KV pages are dynamic and dirty; when evicted they are written to a per-host swap area. Physical HBM is managed as a global page pool, not as fixed per-model block pools. We use a CUDA virtual-memory style mapping so that a logical page can be mapped, unmapped, remapped, or migrated without copying the entire model image; this follows the vTensor/vAttention direction and simultaneously removes the PagedAttention-style pre-allocated pool that prevents redistribution across models. Each GPU has a physical memory budget B_g; the global monitor records for every model m its weight size W_m, estimated active KV footprint K_m, copied-resident flag, loading latency L_m estimated from checkpoint placement, and number of resident replicas.

2. Workload monitor and activity states. For every model m, the monitor maintains a short-term arrival rate, a medium-term arrival rate, queue depth Q_m(t), SLO deadline headroom, and a smoothed idle counter. It classifies each model into one of five states: cold (no weight pages resident), warming (weight prefetch in progress), resident (enough weight pages mapped to begin inference on any replica), runnable (resident and currently has queued requests), and draining (resident but marked for possible demotion). Transitions are governed by two thresholds rather than by individual requests. A model leaves cold and enters warming when its medium-term arrival rate exceeds a low warm-up threshold or when a request arrives and no cold-start-tolerant alternative exists. A resident model is marked draining only after its queue has been empty for an idle_grace period and its predicted activity has fallen below a demotion threshold. A draining model is not immediately evicted; it stays resident until another model actually requires its physical pages. This double-threshold design prevents the micro-idle and brief active-set shifts observed in production traces from triggering a swap.

3. Residency planner. The planner runs every control epoch or whenever the global memory pressure changes signficantly. For each model m it computes a resident utility U_m = (Q_m + alpha * predicted_demand_m) * priority_m / (W_m + expected_KV_m), where Q_m is current queued load, predicted_demand_m comes from the short/medium arrival ratio, priority_m encodes SLO strictness, and alpha balances measured and predicted demand. The planner converts model utilities into a desired replica count: hot models receive at least one replica per logical group that has capacity; medium models receive one replica; cold models receive zero. It then runs a multi-resource best-fit-decreasing algorithm over GPUs. For each GPU, available physical memory is split into a small always-reserved staging buffer and a remainder. The algorithm packs resident model footprints into the remainder, checking that the sum of resident weights plus expected KV of runnable models does not exceed the GPU budget. Because the utility is based on queue pressure, active models are naturally placed on different GPUs when possible, while low-traffic models are co-packed on the same GPU when their combined footprints fit. Space sharing emerges from placing several medium/low-traffic models on one GPU; time sharing emerges when a hot model cannot be co-resident with the current set and needs the full memory of a GPU after the previous occupant is demoted.

4. Eviction and prefetch engine. At every batch boundary, the GPU checks whether any warming or runnable model has a pages-resident deficit. If so, it invokes an eviction policy that selects victims from draining or idle-resident models. The victim selection score is the inverse of U_m times an eviction penalty for being loaded too recently, which prevents thrashing between two models that alternate activity. Weight pages of a victim are clean and are simply unmapped; KV pages are written to host memory before unmapping. Eviction never preempts a running request batch unless the request being scheduled has an SLO deadline that cannot be met otherwise. In that case, the scheduler chooses as preemption victim the resident model whose queued requests have the latest deadlines. The prefetch engine starts loading a model into the staging buffer as soon as the model transitions to warming, before its first request is admitted to the runnable set. Loading uses asynchronous copy and reads from the local checkpoint or, if the checkpoint is not local, from the nearest NVMe/remote secondary copy; this is the only place where time-sharing latency appears, but the residency planner and two-threshold state machine make those occurrences rare and predictable rather than a per-group occurrence.

5. Request-level GPU scheduler. Each GPU runs a local scheduler over the set of resident models. At a scheduling quantum, the scheduler considers every resident model with Q_m > 0 and assigns each request an earliest-deadline-first priority. The scheduler executes the model with the smallest mean laxity, running a bounded-size decode/prefill batch. If a model has no queued work, it is skipped without being unloaded. Therefore, within a control epoch, the GPU may switch its compute between multiple resident models many times, but these switches are pure compute context switches at token/batch granularity, involving no weight movement or request preemption. This is the core departure from QLM, where every consecutive group targeting a different model forces a full swap. In our design the active-set composition can change at request rate while the memory-resident set changes only at the slower residency-planning rate. A model that becomes active and is already resident is served immediately; a model that becomes active but was not predicted is loaded through the prefetch/eviction path, with the planner's threshold on SLO strictness determining whether it should have been kept resident in the first place. The KV cache of each model is allocated on demand from the shared physical page pool, so an idle resident model does not lock up a large KV block pool; only its weight pages remain mapped. When memory pressure from a burst grows, active KV pages are given priority in the page pool, and idle-weight pages are the natural reclamation candidates.

The overall system is closed by a feedback loop: measured SLO miss risk and load latency feed back into priority_m and the predicted_demand_m multiplier; if a model repeatedly becomes active while cold, its resident utility increases until the planner places it in the resident set or co-packs it with another model. Conversely, if a resident model has no requests for multiple grace periods and no predicted activity, its utility decays and it becomes a preferred eviction candidate. In this way the scheduler continuously interpolates between pure space sharing and pure time sharing as a function of instantaneous workload, and never treats an idle model's memory as permanent waste nor a model activation as a synchronous request-group swap.
